questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design end-to-end supply chain controls for Helm charts in a multi-tenant environment, including signature provenance, SBOM coverage, and admission-time enforcement. It also probes per-tenant key management and how to demonstrate both failing and passing cases.

## Key Concepts
- Helm chart signing with cosign
- SBOM generation for chart dependencies
- Rekor attestations
- Kyverno/OPA admission policies
- Tenant-specific key management and verification
- Local and CI verification workflows

## Code Example
```yaml
# minimal GitHub Actions gate (high level)
name: Sign and Verify Helm Chart
on: [push]
jobs:
  sign-verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Set up cosign
        run: cosign version
      - name: Sign chart
        run: cosign sign --key cosign-keys/${{ env.TENANT }}.key charts/myapp-0.1.0.tgz
      - name: Generate SBOM
        run: syft chart:charts/myapp-0.1.0.tgz -o cyclonedx-json
      - name: Rekor attestation
        run: cosign attach to Rekor
      - name: Publish verification results
        run: echo verified
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you rotate tenant keys with minimal blast radius?
- What are failure modes if the SBOM is missing or signatures don’t verify?

## Why This Is Asked

Tests integration of policy-as-code, attestation, and runtime security across a multi-tenant cluster. Candidates must show how to bind OPA, Kyverno, Rekor/cosign, and Falco to a coherent workflow, plus a concrete verification plan.

## Key Concepts

- Image provenance and attestations (cosign, Rekor)
- Policy-as-code (OPA, Kyverno)
- Runtime security (Falco/eBPF)
- Multi-tenant governance and testability

## Code Example

```javascript
// OPA Rego (conceptual)
package kubernetes.admission
violation[reason] {
  input.review.object.kind == "Pod"
  image := input.review.object.spec.containers[_].image
  not imageIsAttested(image)
  reason = "image provenance missing"
}
```

```javascript
// Kyverno policy (conceptual)
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-provenance-and-security
spec:
  validationFailureAction: enforce
  rules:
  - name: require-nonroot
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Pod"]
    validate:
      message: "must set runAsNonRoot and readOnlyRootFilesystem"
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - securityContext:
              runAsNonRoot: true
  - name: require-attested-image
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Pod"]
    validate:
      message: "image must have Rekor cosign attestation"
      pattern:
        spec:
          containers:
          - image: "*attested*"
```

```javascript
// Falco rule (conceptual)
- rule: Unsigned Image Usage
  condition: container.image.signature == ""
  output: "Unsigned image detected: %container.image.repository"
  priority: WARN
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you handle attestation key rotation?
- How would you measure false positives and performance impact?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests a beginner-friendly, practical security gate focused on container runtime privileges in Kubernetes manifests.

## Key Concepts
- PodSecurityContext vs Container securityContext
- readOnlyRootFilesystem, runAsNonRoot, runAsUser
- PrivilegeEscalation and privileged flag in containers
- GitHub Actions as a gating mechanism

## Code Example
```yaml
# Failing manifest
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: fail
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: example/app:latest
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: false
          runAsUser: 0
          privileged: true
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: true
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: false
```
```yaml
# Passing manifest
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: pass

  template:
    spec:

```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Multi-tenant clusters need strict API access control; SPIFFE identity ensures only trusted services can perform sensitive calls. Gatekeeper + OPA enforces runtime policy with centralized visibility.

## Key Concepts
- OPA Gatekeeper
- ConstraintTemplate and Constraint
- SPIFFE IDs and SVIDs
- Kubernetes API verbs and RBAC implications
- Validation via audit logs and Gatekeeper status

## Code Example
```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8sapicnst
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sApiConstraint
  targets:
    - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
      rego: |
        package k8sapi
        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          input.review.kind.kind == "Pod"
          input.review.object.metadata.namespace != "monitoring"
          not allowed_spiffe(input.review.object)
          msg := sprintf("Pod %s in namespace %s cannot use API verb %s", [input.review.object.metadata.name, input.review.object.metadata.namespace, input.review.operation])
        }
        allowed_spiffe(pod) {
          pod.metadata.annotations["spiffe.io/spiffe-id"]
          pod.metadata.annotations["spiffe.io/spiffe-id"] in data.constraint.spec.allowedSVIDs
        }
```

```yaml
# Constraint
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sApiConstraint
metadata:
  name: restrict-api-verbs
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny
  allowedSVIDs:
    - "spiffe://ibm.com/workload/web"
    - "spiffe://tesla.com/workload/monitor"
    - "spiffe://cloudflare.com/workload/edge"
```

## Validation Plan
1. Deploy ConstraintTemplate and Constraint
2. Test compliant GET request from approved SPIFFE ID
3. Test noncompliant POST request from unapproved SPIFFE ID
4. Verify denial in Gatekeeper audit logs
5. Confirm monitoring namespace bypass works correctly

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests policy design, RBAC scoping, and CI integration for a high-sensitivity platform.

## Key Concepts

- Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate and Constraint
- RBAC bindings (RoleBinding, ClusterRoleBinding)
- Namespace-scoped allowlists and auditing in CI

## Code Example

```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate (RBACWhitelist)
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: rbacwhitelist
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names: {}
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package rbacwhitelist
      violation[{msg}] {
        binding := input.review.object
        binding.kind == \"RoleBinding\" or binding.kind == \"ClusterRoleBinding\"
        role := binding.roleRef.name
        ns := binding.metadata.namespace
        allowed := data.allowlist[ns]
        role != \"\"; role notin allowed
        msg := sprintf(\"RBAC violation: %s bound to %s in %s\", [binding.kind, role, ns])
      }
```

```yaml
# Constraint (per-namespace allowlist)
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: RbacWhitelist
metadata:
  name: rbac-whitelist-prod
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
    - apiGroups: [\"rbac.authorization.k8s.io\"]
      kinds: [\"RoleBinding\", \"ClusterRoleBinding\"]
  parameters:
    namespaceAllowlists:
      production: [\"view\", \"edit\"]
      staging: [\"view\"]
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you test this with CI/CD and simulate violations?
- How would you handle dynamic/temporary permissions without conflicting with the allowlist?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical data validation in CI/CD with a concrete schema and gating.

## Key Concepts
- CSV header validation
- Type coercion and data quality
- CI gate integration (GitHub Actions)

## Code Example
```python
import csv, sys
from datetime import datetime

EXPECTED = {
  'id': int,
  'date': 'date',
  'amount': float,
  'category': str
}

DATE_FMT = '%Y-%m-%d'

def parse_row(row):
  row['id'] = int(row['id'])
  row['date'] = datetime.strptime(row['date'], DATE_FMT).date()
  row['amount'] = float(row['amount'])
  row['category'] = str(row['category'])
  return row

def main(path):
  with open(path, newline='') as f:
    reader = csv.DictReader(f)
    header = set(reader.fieldnames or [])
    if header != set(EXPECTED.keys()):
      print('Header mismatch:', reader.fieldnames)
      sys.exit(1)
    for r in reader:
      try:
        parse_row(r)
      except Exception as e:
        print('Type/Parse error', e, r)
        sys.exit(1)
  print('OK')

if __name__ == '__main__':
  sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1]))
```

- How would you test locally with representative failing/passing CSVs?

## Why This Is Asked

Immutability of container images is a core security practice. This checks a tangible gating mechanism candidates can implement in a simple CI step.

## Key Concepts

- YAML manifest parsing
- Image digest pinning (immutable refs)
- Lightweight CI scripts in GitHub Actions
- Local verification parity with CI

## Code Example

```yaml
# .github/workflows/pin-digest.yml
name: Pin Image Digests
on:
  push:
    paths:
      - '**/*.yaml'
      - '**/*.yml'
jobs:
  digest_check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Install jq and yq
        run: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y jq wget
      - name: Install yq
        run: wget -qO- https://github.com/mikefarah/yq/releases/download/v4.25.1/yq_linux_amd64 -O /usr/bin/yq && chmod +x /usr/bin/yq
      - name: Validate image digests
        run: |
          DIGESTED=$(yq -r '.. | .image? // empty' **/*.yaml **/*.yml | grep -v '^$' )
          if echo "$DIGESTED" | grep -vq '@sha256:'; then
            echo "Found image refs without digest:";
            echo "$DIGESTED"; exit 1;
          fi
          echo "All images pinned to digests."
```

## Why This Is Asked

In production Kubernetes environments, ensuring supply-chain security for Helm-based deployments is critical. This question evaluates your ability to integrate multiple security tools—Helm templating, SBOM generation, and image signature verification—into a cohesive CI gate. It tests practical knowledge of enforcing provenance and attestations before code merges.

## Key Concepts

- **Helm templating and values extraction**: Rendering charts to discover all container images referenced in deployments
- **SBOM generation**: Using Syft to create a CycloneDX SBOM that catalogs all dependencies and artifacts
- **Image signing verification**: Using cosign to validate container image signatures against a public key stored in the repository
- **CI gate integration**: Implementing fail-fast behavior in GitHub Actions to block unsigned images and missing attestations

## Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal GitHub Actions workflow for Helm image signing enforcement
name: Helm Image Security Gate

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  helm-security:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install cosign
        uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@v3

      - name: Install Helm and Syft
        run: |
          curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash
          curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anchore/syft/main/install.sh | sh

      - name: Render Helm templates
        run: helm template my-app ./chart --values values.yaml --output-dir ./rendered

      - name: Extract image references
        run: |
          grep -rh 'image:' ./rendered | awk '{print $2}' > images.txt

      - name: Generate SBOM with Syft
        run: |
          syft $(cat images.txt) -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json

      - name: Verify image signatures with cosign
        run: |
          COSIGN_PUBLIC_KEY=cosign.pub
          for IMAGE in $(cat images.txt); do
            cosign verify --key $COSIGN_PUBLIC_KEY $IMAGE || exit 1
          done
```

## Why This Is Asked

This question evaluates practical understanding of Kubernetes security primitives including RBAC, ServiceAccount isolation, PodSecurityContext, and admission controls—essential skills for securing containerized workloads.

## Key Concepts

- **Namespace-scoped RBAC**: Role and RoleBinding for resource access control within specific namespaces
- **ServiceAccount isolation**: Dedicated service accounts to separate pod identities and permissions
- **PodSecurityContext**: Security constraints including runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, readOnlyRootFilesystem, and capability dropping
- **Admission controls**: PodSecurity standards and OPA Gatekeeper for policy enforcement at admission time

## Code Example

```yaml
# ServiceAccount (dev)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: data-processor-sa
  namespace: dev
---
# Role for read-only access to ConfigMaps and Secrets
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: data-processor-role
  namespace: dev
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["configmaps", "secrets"]
  verbs: ["get", "list"]
---
# RoleBinding
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: data-processor-binding
  namespace: dev
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: data-processor-sa
  namespace: dev
roleRef:
  kind: Role
  name: data-processor-role
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you test the RBAC permissions locally?
- What changes are needed for the prod namespace?
- How would you implement network policies alongside these security controls?
